Title: Subword enumeration up to stack-sorting equivalence
Text:
Subword enumeration up to stack-sorting equivalence
John M. Campbell
Narad Rampersad
Abstract
Defant and Kravitz introduced generalizations of West’s stack-
sorting map s from permutations to finite words. This raises questions
as to how such generalizations could be applied in the field of combi-
natorics on words. The Defant–Kravitz generalizations of s depend on
how repeated occurrences of the same character within a word may
be repositioned, according to their tortoise and hare operations. As
demonstrated in this paper, these operations provide a natural way of
extending abelian complexity functions for infinite sequences, in a way
that gives light to structural properties associated with infinite words.
We apply these new ideas to two famous infinite words: the paperfold-
ing word and the Thue–Morse word. In the case of the Thue–Morse
word, we discover an interesting connection to the previous work of
several authors, such as de Luca and Varricchio, on the “special” fac-
tors of the Thue–Morse word. This may be seen as providing a basis
for a new and interdisciplinary area linking the combinatorics about
the stack-sorting of permutations with the field of combinatorics on
words.
MSC: 05A05, 68R15, 11B85
Keywords: subword, complexity function, permutation, stack sorting, partial sorting algo-
rithm, West’s stack-sorting map, automatic sequence, paperfolding sequence, Thue–Morse
sequence, Walnut, k-abelian complexity

Introduction
What is referred to as West’s stack-sorting map traces back to Knuth’s classic
texts on computer programming [23, §2.2.1] and was given, in an equivalent
way, in 1990 in a seminal PhD thesis [32]. Since partial sorting algorithms on
permutations helped to lead toward areas in combinatorics devoted to per-
mutation patterns, this, in turn, motivates the extension of such algorithms
to combinatorial objects generalizing permutations. In this paper, we show

For a permutation σ of {1, 2, . . . , n}, let σ be written as a word in
{1, 2, . . . , n}∗so that
σ = LnR
(1)
for possibly empty subwords L and R. West’s stack-sorting map s may be
defined so that s maps the empty permutation to the same permutation and
so that
s(σ) = s(L)s(R)n.
(2)
From the recursion in (2), we see that s is defined only on words consisting of
distinct and positive integers. This raises questions as to how the recurrence
relation in (2) could be generalized so as to define stack-sorting operations on
words with possibly repeated characters, and Defant and Kravitz [19] were
the first to introduce and apply such generalizations. In view of research
works subsequent and related to the Defant–Kravitz generalizations of s [9,
11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18], it appears that these generalizations have
not been applied directly in the study of automatic sequences or in terms
of complexity functions on infinite words/sequences. This forms the main
purpose of our paper.
As in the work of Defant and Kravitz [19], we express how the extension
of s from permutations to words is inspired by many past research efforts
on the extension of the study of pattern avoidance in permutations to pat-
tern avoidance in words, together with past research on sorting procedures on
words. Ideally, through new applications of and investigations devoted to the
application of sorting procedures on finite subwords of automatic sequences,
this could lead toward a deeper understanding of aspects about such sub-
words in terms of, say, growth properties when it comes to the enumeration
of subwords up to a given point in an automatic sequence, or in terms of, for
example, Morse–Hedlund-type results (cf. [28]) characterizing eventual peri-
odicity or periodicity-like conditions in terms of the behavior of complexity
functions.
For a given sequence x, it is of interest in its own right how equal-length
subwords of x relate to one another in terms of partial sortings of or reposi-
tionings of characters. The notion of stack-sorting equivalence on subwords
introduced in this paper helps to formalize this idea and provides applica-
tions based on this idea to the automatic sequences known as the paperfolding
2


sequence and the Thue–Morse sequence.

2.2
The complexity of automatic sequences
For a full background on automatic sequences, we cite the standard text on
automatic sequences [3]. Informally, the inherently recursive nature of auto-
matic sequences can be thought of as reflecting how the study of subwords
of such sequences helps to give light to the nature of such sequences and
the applications of such sequences within number theory and computer sci-
ence. This is reflected in a number of recent, notable research publications
concerning complexity functions on automatic sequences, as in the work of
Golafshan et al. on the k-binomial complexity for generalized Thue–Morse
sequences [21], the work of L¨u et al. on the 2-binomial complexity of general-
ized Thue–Morse sequences [25], the work of Shallit on the cyclic complexity
of the Thue–Morse sequence [31], the work of Rampersad on the periodic
complexity of the Thue–Morse sequence, the Rudin–Shapiro sequence, and
the period-doubling sequence [29], and the work of Lejeune et al. on the
k-binomial complexity of the Thue–Morse sequence [24].
Two of the most basic and prototypical instances of non-periodic auto-
matic sequences are the Thue–Morse sequence and the paperfolding sequence.
While it is well-known that the abelian complexity of the Thue–Morse se-
quence is 2-periodic, the abelian complexity function of the paperfolding
sequence is non-periodic and 2-regular, as proved by Madill and Rampersad
[27]. This motivates the material in Section 5 below on a new, abelian-like
complexity function applied to the paperfolding sequence. In Section 6, we
5


investigate this abelian-like complexity function as applied to the TM se-
quence, uncovering an unexpected connection with the work of de Luca and
Varricchio [26] concerning distinguished factors of the TM sequence.
From the equivalence in (7) for a given binary word b, we restrict our
attention to how Defant and Kravitz’s tortoise operation can be used to
extend abelian complexity functions, and this leads us to Section 3 below.

Tortoise complexity and left special factors
A crucial tool in the study of subword complexity functions is the notion of
“special” subwords. If x is an infinite word then a subword w of x is right
special (sometimes just special) if there are distinct letters of the alphabet
a and b such that both wa and wb are subwords of x. Similarly, if both aw
and bw are subwords of x, then w is left special. Left special subwords are
also relevant to the computation of ρt
x(n) in the following way:
Lemma 1. Let w and w′ be distinct equal-length subwords of an infinite
binary word x such that w ∼t w′. Suppose w and w′ each contain at least
one 1 and write w = uv and w′ = u′v, where both u and u′ contain exactly
one 1. Then zv is a left special subword of x, where z is the longest common
suffix of u and u′.
8


Proof. Since z is the longest common suffix of u and u′, it is preceded by
different letters in u and u′; hence, zv is left special.
Consider an infinite binary word x where the 1’s occur with bounded gaps;
i.e., there exists a constant B such that every factor of x of length B contains
a 1.
Theorem 1. Let x be an infinite binary word such that ρx(n) ∈O(n) and
the 1’s in x occur with bounded gaps. There exists a constant C such that
ρx(n) −C ≤ρt
x(n) ≤ρx(n)
for all sufficiently large n.
Proof. Consider a ∼t-equivalence class of x containing at least two distinct
words w and w′ of length n. Suppose further that w and w′ contain at least
one 1. Applying Lemma 1, write w = xy and w′ = x′y, where y is left special
and x and x′ each contain exactly one 1. Let |y| = m. Note that since the
1’s in x occur with bounded gaps, there is a bounded number of choices for
x and x′, which implies that there is a bounded number of possibilities for
m.
Now, note that the number of left special factors of length m is equal
to ρx(m + 1) −ρx(m) if the prefix of x of length m occurs at least twice
in x and is equal to ρx(m + 1) −ρx(m) + 1 otherwise. A deep result of
Cassaigne [7] states that ρx(m) ∈O(m) if and only if there is a constant
D such that ρx(m + 1) −ρx(m) ≤D for all m. Hence, not only is there a
bounded number of possibilities for the length of the left special factor y, but
for each possible length there are at most D + 1 choices for y.
The conclusion is that there is a bounded number of ∼t-equivalence classes
of x that contain more than one element, and furthermore, the size of such
classes is bounded as well. This is sufficient to establish the claim.
Much is known about the right special subwords of the Thue–Morse word
t. It is well-known that if w is a subword of t then so is the reversal of w,
denoted wR. It follows that if w is a right special subword of t then wR is
a left special subword of t. De Luca and Varricchio gave a formula for the
number of right special factors of t of length n. The same applies to left
special factors by our earlier observation, so from [26, Lemma 4.3] we get the
following fact.

Theorem 4. Let n be an integer such that n ≥9. If there are length-n
subwords v ̸= w of t such that v ∼t w, then {v, w} = {01y, 10y}, where y is
left special.
Proof. Since n ≥9, v and w each have at least two 1’s. Write v = uz and
w = u′z where z begins with a 1 and u and u′ each contain exactly one 1.
Note that |u| ≤4 and |z| ≥5. Since t is a concatenation of 01’s and 10’s
and does not contain 01010 or 10101, if z is a factor of t of length at least
5, then the positions of every occurrence of z in t have the same parity. We
have two cases:
Case 1: z occurs at a position of even parity. Then either u = 01 and
u′ = 10 or vice-versa and y = z is left special.
Case 2: z occurs at a position of odd parity. Since z begins with a 1,
either u = 010 and u′ = 100 or vice-versa and y = 0z is left special.

an occurrence of either v or w in t. Note the two cases in the statement of

Abstract: Defant and Kravitz introduced generalizations of West’s stack- sorting map s from permutations to finite words. This raises questions as to how such generalizations could be applied in the field of combi- natorics on words. The Defant–Kravitz generalizations of s depend on how repeated occurrences of the same character within a word may be repositioned, according to their tortoise and hare operations. As demonstrated in this paper, these operations provide a natural way of extending abelian complexity functions for infinite sequences, in a way that gives light to structural properties associated with infinite words. We apply these new ideas to two famous infinite words: the paperfold- ing word and the Thue–Morse word. In the case of the Thue–Morse word, we discover an interesting connection to the previous work of several authors, such as de Luca and Varricchio, on the “special” fac- tors of the Thue–Morse word. This may be seen as providing a basis for a new and interdisciplinary area linking the combinatorics about the stack-sorting of permutations with the field of combinatorics on words.
